title: Subset Sum
directAnswer: Decide whether some subset of the array sums to exactly T. It's the feasibility flavor of 0/1 knapsack: dp[s] is true if some subset hits sum s. The recurrence is dp[s] = dp[s] OR dp[s - num] for each number, sweeping s DESCENDING so each number is used at most once. Anchor dp[0] = true (the empty subset). O(n·T) time, O(T) space — or fold the whole row into one big integer and use bitset shifts.

rules: It's a **boolean** DP: `dp[s]` answers 'is sum `s` reachable by some subset?' — you OR possibilities together, you don't add counts.
Sweep the sum **DESCENDING** (`T → num`) in the 1-D version so each number is used at most once. Ascending would allow reuse (that's the unbounded/coin-change-II variant).
Anchor `dp[0] = true` — the empty subset sums to 0. Every reachable sum chains back to this.
Once `dp[T]` becomes true you can stop early; and if `T` exceeds the total of all positives it's instantly false.
The **bitset trick** packs the whole `dp[]` row into one integer: `bits |= bits << num` does all `T` OR-updates in a single shift, and bit `T` of the result is the answer.
whenToUse: Pure yes/no: does a subset hit an exact target sum?
Partitioning a set into two equal-sum halves (target = total / 2)
Reachability over sums rather than optimizing a value
n and T are small enough that O(n·T) is affordable (pseudo-polynomial)
antiSignals: You need the COUNT of subsets hitting T → counting DP (sum of ways, not OR)
Numbers reusable any number of times → unbounded variant, sweep ascending
You must return the actual subset → track parent pointers / backtrack the table
T is astronomically large → O(n·T) infeasible; try meet-in-the-middle (O(2^{n/2}))
remember.takeaway: Subset Sum is 0/1 knapsack with the objective swapped from 'max value' to 'is it reachable?'. The boolean recurrence dp[s] |= dp[s - num], swept descending, is the skeleton behind Partition Equal Subset Sum, Target Sum, and Last Stone Weight II. The bitset shift (bits |= bits << num) is the trick that makes it blazingly fast in practice.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize a feasibility question as boolean 0/1 knapsack, get the descending 1-D sweep right (each item once), and ideally know the bitset speedup.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Sweeping the sum ascending (which reuses numbers and answers a different problem), or forgetting dp[0] = true so no sum is ever reachable.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name it as 0/1 knapsack feasibility, derive dp[s] |= dp[s - num] descending, then offer the bitset form (bits |= bits << num) as the one-line speedup and explain why bit T is the answer.

problemStatement:
You are given an array `nums` of positive integers and a target integer `T`.

Determine whether there exists a ***subset*** of `nums` whose elements sum to exactly `T`. Each element may be used **at most once** (it's either in the subset or not).

Return `true` if such a subset exists, otherwise `false`.
understanding: Answer a pure yes/no question: can any combination of the given numbers, each used once, add up to T? There's no value to maximize — only reachability of the target sum. It is the feasibility (boolean) version of 0/1 knapsack, where the 'capacity' is the target and the 'value' question becomes 'is this sum attainable?'.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a number be used more than once?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — each element at most once. That's the 0/1 constraint and dictates the descending 1-D sweep. Reuse would be a different (unbounded) problem.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are all numbers positive?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes here. Negatives would let sums grow unbounded in both directions and require an offset or a different state space.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the empty subset count?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The empty subset sums to 0, so T = 0 is always true. That's exactly the base case dp[0] = true.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need to return the subset itself?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — just whether one exists. Returning the actual subset would require backtracking through the DP table or tracking parents.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can T be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 10⁴ here, so an O(n·T) table of ~2×10⁶ booleans is fine. If T were ~10⁹ we'd need meet-in-the-middle instead.

examples.explanation: The subset {4, 5} sums to 9 (so does {3, 4, 2}). At least one subset hits the target.
Excluding 34 (which alone exceeds 30), the rest total only 3 + 4 + 12 + 5 + 2 = 26 < 30. No subset reaches 30.
The subset {11} works, and so does {1, 5, 5}. Either makes the target reachable.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree to run before writing code. Subset Sum lands on the boolean 1-D DP (descending) branch.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recursive Include/Exclude
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to establish the take-or-skip recurrence on the remaining target, then flag the 2ⁿ branching.
hints: Look at the LAST number. You either include it in the subset or you don't. What target remains in each case?
Exclude it: still need to make T from the first n-1 numbers. Include it (only if num ≤ rem): need to make rem - num from the first n-1.
can(i, rem) = can(i-1, rem) OR can(i-1, rem - num[i]). Base: rem == 0 → true; i < 0 → (rem == 0).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each number forks into include/exclude, so the recursion tree has up to 2ⁿ leaves, each doing O(1) work. Recursion depth is O(n).
approaches.explanation:
Decide the numbers one at a time, from the last index down. For number `i` there are two futures: **exclude** it and try to form the same `rem` from numbers `0..i-1`, or **include** it (only when `num[i] <= rem`) and try to form `rem - num[i]` from `0..i-1`. The answer is the OR of those two — a subset exists if *either* branch can finish the job.

**The mental shift: a yes/no reachability question, decided one element at a time.** Unlike knapsack's `max`, there's nothing to optimize here — we only care whether *some* path reaches `rem == 0`. So we combine the two branches with logical OR: if any sequence of include/exclude decisions zeroes out the remaining target, the whole thing is true.

**Why the include branch recurses on `i-1`.** Moving to the previous index after taking number `i` is what enforces 'each element at most once' — the same number can never be picked again. Recursing on `i` instead would allow reuse (the unbounded variant).

**Why the guard `num[i] <= rem`.** Including a number bigger than the remaining target would drive `rem` negative, which can never come back to 0 with positive numbers — so we simply don't take that branch.

**The base cases.** `rem == 0` means we've already hit the target exactly — return true immediately, even with numbers to spare. Running out of numbers with `rem > 0` is false.

**Why we don't ship this.** The same `(i, rem)` state recurs through many include/exclude orderings — exponential overlap on two small state variables. Cache it and the blowup collapses to O(n·T).
approaches.insight: The state is two numbers — how many elements remain to decide and how much target is left — and the naive tree recomputes the same `(i, rem)` repeatedly. Two bounded state variables plus heavy overlap is the textbook signal for an O(n·T) DP; the only difference from knapsack is OR instead of max.

python.explanation: No numbers left and target unmet → false.
Include branch only when nums[i] fits, recursing on i-1 (single use).
OR the two branches — reachability, not optimization.

edgeCases.behavior: can(i, 0) returns true immediately — the empty subset works.

pitfalls: Recursing on i (not i-1) in the include branch — allows reuse, solving a different problem.
Using AND or max instead of OR — this is a feasibility question, so OR the branches.
Skipping this approach — the include/exclude recurrence is what the interviewer wants to hear first.

approaches.name: Top-Down Memoization on (index, remaining target)
approaches.whenToMention: The fix once you name the overlap — 'cache the answer for each (index, remaining target)'.
hints: can(i, rem) returns the same boolean every call. Cache it in a 2-D table indexed by index and remaining target.
Use a memo of size n × (T+1); store a tri-state (unknown / true / false) since the answer is boolean.
memo[i][rem] = can(i-1, rem) OR can(i-1, rem - num[i]); fill it before returning so each state is solved once.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are n × (T+1) distinct (i, rem) states, each resolved once in O(1) → O(n·T) time. The memo is O(n·T); recursion depth is O(n) on top.
approaches.explanation:
Keep the include/exclude recurrence but cache `can(i, rem)` so each `(index, remaining target)` is solved exactly once. Because the result is boolean, use a tri-state memo (unknown / true / false) — `Integer`/`Boolean` objects with `null` in Java, or `@lru_cache` in Python.

**The mental shift: the answer depends only on (i, rem).** Whatever include/exclude path led here, the question 'can the first `i` numbers make `rem`?' has a fixed answer. Caching by `(i, rem)` collapses all the duplicate subtrees, and the number of distinct states — `n × (T+1)` — is the time bound.

**Why the state is two-dimensional.** As in 0/1 knapsack (and unlike Coin Change), the answer depends on *both* how many numbers remain and the remaining target — which numbers are still available changes what's reachable. So the memo needs both axes.

**Why a tri-state, not a plain boolean default.** A default `false` can't be distinguished from 'computed and found false', so you'd recompute false states forever. Mark cells unknown until filled (e.g. `null`).

**A language note worth saying out loud.** The top-down version recurses up to `n` deep. In Java that's fine for `n ≤ 200`. In Python the default recursion limit is about 1000, so deep top-down DP can raise `RecursionError` on large `n` — which is exactly why the bottom-up boolean table (next approach) is the safer default in Python and also unlocks the bitset speedup.
approaches.insight: Same mechanical DP upgrade as every problem here: a correct recurrence plus a cache keyed on the true state, `(index, remaining target)`. The boolean objective just means the cached value is a yes/no, and the table size is your complexity.

dryRun.intro: memo[i][rem] caches whether the first i numbers can make rem. Filled lazily from the last index.

java.explanation: Boolean objects default to null = 'unknown', distinct from a computed true/false.
Cache hit — return the stored reachability for this (index, target) in O(1).
Only try the include branch if exclude failed and the number fits — short-circuits work.
Store the resolved boolean before returning so this state is never recomputed.

python.explanation: Caches can by its (i, rem) arguments — a clean tri-state top-down memo.
Exclude branch first; if it already succeeds, short-circuit and return true.
Include branch. Note: recursion depth up to n can hit Python's ~1000 limit — prefer the bottom-up table for large n.

edgeCases.behavior: can(i, 0) returns true immediately — empty subset.

edgeCases.input: T larger than the array total
edgeCases.behavior: Every path runs out of numbers with rem > 0 → false, cached cheaply.

pitfalls: Defaulting the memo to false instead of a separate 'unknown' marker — recomputes false states.
Sizing the memo as T instead of T+1 — sums 0..T need T+1 columns.
Deep recursion in Python (depth ~n) can exceed the ~1000 recursion limit — tabulation avoids the stack.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up Boolean DP + Bitset Trick (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Build the boolean dp[] swept DESCENDING, then offer the bitset one-liner as the fast variant.
hints: Make dp[s] = true if some subset sums to s. dp[0] = true; everything else false.
For each number, update dp[s] = dp[s] OR dp[s - num] for s from T down to num. Descending order keeps each number single-use.
Speedup: represent the whole dp[] row as the bits of one big integer. Then dp[s] |= dp[s - num] for all s at once is just bits |= (bits << num). Bit T of the final integer is the answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The outer loop runs n times, the inner sum loop up to T → O(n·T) time, O(T) space for a single boolean row. The bitset form does the same O(n·T) bit operations but processes ~64 sums per machine word, so it's roughly T/64 times faster in practice.
approaches.explanation:
Build reachability from the ground up. `dp[s]` is true when some subset sums to exactly `s`. Anchor `dp[0] = true` (the empty subset), then fold in numbers one at a time: a sum `s` becomes reachable if it was already reachable *or* if `s - num` was reachable before this number was added (then adding `num` lands on `s`). That's `dp[s] = dp[s] OR dp[s - num]`. The answer is `dp[T]`.

**Why the 1-D sweep must go DESCENDING — the crux.** With a single `dp[]` array, when we process a number we must read `dp[s - num]` as it was *before* this number was folded in. Iterating `s` from `T` down to `num` guarantees `dp[s - num]` still holds the pre-number value, so each number contributes to a sum at most once. Sweep ascending and `dp[s - num]` may already include the current number, letting it be reused — that's the unbounded / Coin-Change-II variant, a different problem. This is the exact same loop-direction rule as 0/1 knapsack.

**Why dp[0] = true is load-bearing.** Every reachable sum is built by adding numbers onto the empty subset. If `dp[0]` were false, no sum could ever flip to true and the answer would always be false. That single anchored cell makes the whole array meaningful.

**The bitset trick.** Notice the update `dp[s] |= dp[s - num]` is the *same* shift applied to every `s`. So pack the entire row into one big integer where bit `s` means 'sum `s` reachable'. Adding a number is then a single operation: `bits |= bits << num` shifts every reachable sum up by `num` and ORs it back in — performing all `T` updates at once. After processing every number, check bit `T`: `(bits >> T) & 1`. Python's arbitrary-precision integers make this trivial; in Java a `BigInteger` does the same. It's the same O(n·T) work, but the machine handles ~64 sums per word, giving a large constant-factor speedup.

**Why no descending worry with the bitset.** The shift-and-OR builds a fresh value from the old `bits`, so it inherently uses the pre-number state — there's no in-place left-to-right hazard to guard against.
approaches.insight: Subset Sum is 0/1 knapsack with the objective swapped from max-value to boolean reachability — and the descending sweep is the shared signature of 'each item once'. The bitset reformulation is the portable trick worth memorizing: when a DP row is a set of reachable integers updated by a constant shift, a big-integer `bits |= bits << k` does the whole row in one instruction. The same boolean skeleton solves Partition Equal Subset Sum and underlies Target Sum.

java.line: for (int s = T; s >= num; s--) {
java.explanation: DESCENDING sum sweep — dp[s - num] keeps its pre-number value, so each number is used at most once.
Sum s is reachable if it already was, or if s - num was reachable before adding num.
Shift every reachable sum up by num and OR back — all T updates in one bit operation.

python.explanation: Base case: empty subset reaches sum 0.
Reverse range = descending sweep, enforcing single use of each number.
Big-int bitset: one shift-or performs the whole dp row update. Python ints are arbitrary precision, so this just works.
Bit T set means a subset sums to exactly T.

edgeCases.behavior: dp[0] = true returned directly — empty subset.
Folding that number sets dp[T] = dp[0] = true.

edgeCases.input: T exceeds total of all numbers
edgeCases.behavior: dp[T] never flips → false (the bitset simply never sets bit T).

pitfalls: Sweeping the sum ASCENDING — reuses numbers, answering the unbounded variant instead of 0/1.
Forgetting dp[0] = true — then no sum is ever reachable and the answer is always false.
In Java, using a fixed-width long as the bitset when T > 63 — overflow; use BigInteger (or a long[] bitset) for T up to 10⁴.

commonMistakes: Sweeping the sum ascending in the 1-D version, reusing numbers and solving a different (unbounded) problem.
Forgetting to set dp[0] = true, so no sum is ever reachable.
Using a 64-bit integer as the bitset when the target exceeds 63 — silent overflow.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Ascending sum sweep reuses numbers
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Iterating s low-to-high updates dp[s - num] before you read it, so the same number folds in twice — that's the unbounded variant. Descending order preserves the pre-number values.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing dp[0] = true
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Every reachable sum is built by adding numbers onto the empty subset. If dp[0] starts false, the OR never has a true to propagate and dp[T] stays false for every input.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Fixed-width bitset overflow
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A single Java long holds only 64 bits, so 'bits |= bits << num' silently drops sums above 63. For T up to 10⁴ you need BigInteger (or an explicit long[] of ceil((T+1)/64) words).

followupVariations.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
followupVariations.hint: Subset Sum with T = total / 2 (and total must be even) — the canonical application of this boolean DP.

followupVariations.title: Target Sum
followupVariations.hint: Assign +/− signs to every number — reduces to counting subsets with a fixed sum, a counting cousin of this DP.

followupVariations.title: Last Stone Weight II
followupVariations.hint: Minimize the difference of two groups — find the reachable subset sum closest to total / 2.

followupVariations.title: Count of Subsets with Sum T
followupVariations.hint: Swap the boolean OR for an integer sum: dp[s] += dp[s - num], counting subsets instead of testing existence.

patternNote: Canonical 0/1 knapsack feasibility — boolean reachable-sums DP. Recognize it whenever the question is 'can a subset hit an exact sum?' with each element used once. The descending sweep marks it as 0/1, and the same skeleton powers Partition Equal Subset Sum, Last Stone Weight II, and (with OR→sum) the counting variants. The bitset shift is the practical speedup.
